meta.descriptionEn: On the morning of November 7, 1940, a brand-new suspension bridge in Washington State began to ripple, then twist, in what engineers call only a moderate wind. Just four months after opening, it was gone. Why did a bridge nicknamed Galloping Gertie move from its very first days? Who chose its slim, elegant design, and why did a famous engineer predict failure while it was still being built? And why do so many physics textbooks still give the wrong explanation? Using wind tunnel tests, an official inquiry and rare surviving film, this documentary follows the full story of Tacoma Narrows, and how one dramatic failure changed the way every long bridge since has been designed.

Is bridge ko Galloping Gertie kyun kaha jata tha? Iska design kis ne banaya aur kya ghalti hui? Kya yeh resonance tha ya kuch aur? Is documentary mein hum film, inquiry aur wind tunnel tests ki roshni mein poori kahani dekhenge, aur yeh bhi ke is hadse ne aaj ke bridges ka design kaise badal diya.

articleEn: It is the morning of 7 November 1940 at the Tacoma Narrows in Washington State. The wind is strong, and a brand-new suspension bridge is moving in a strange way. At about 9:45, the bridge deck is not just bobbing up and down but twisting. The wind is blowing at roughly 40 miles per hour. On the roadway, a car slides uncontrollably from side to side. Its driver is Leonard Coatsworth, an editor at the newspaper The News Tribune. Coatsworth abandons the car and crawls on his hands and knees for more than 500 yards to reach the towers.
Then, at about 11 o'clock, the entire main span falls into the waters of Puget Sound. The bridge, which had opened only four months earlier, is gone.

The question is how a completely new bridge could collapse in a wind of only 40 mph. Did the engineers make some enormous mistake? Many physics textbooks present the collapse as an example of resonance, but later research says the story was far more complex. The disaster changed bridge engineering forever, and it still influences the design of every long-span bridge today. So let's start at the beginning with the full story of Galloping Gertie, from the dream to the destruction, and then the lessons that followed.

articleEn: Between the city of Tacoma and the Kitsap Peninsula lies a narrow waterway of Puget Sound called the Tacoma Narrows. The idea of building a bridge here was very old. As early as 1889, the Northern Pacific Railway proposed a railway trestle. Serious efforts, however, began in the mid-1920s. In 1923 the Tacoma Chamber of Commerce launched a campaign for the bridge and also funded various studies.

During this period, several well-known bridge engineers were consulted. Among them was Joseph B. Strauss, who later became chief engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge. Another was David B. Steinman, who later designed the Mackinac Bridge. Steinman made several visits and presented a preliminary proposal in 1929. But by 1931 the Chamber had ended the agreement, saying that Steinman was not working hard enough to secure funding.

Then came 1937. The Washington State legislature created the Washington State Toll Bridge Authority and, at the request of Tacoma and Pierce County, set aside 5,000 dollars for a study. But money problems were there from the start. The income from the proposed tolls was not enough to cover construction costs. There was another expense too: the contract of a private company that ran a ferry across the Narrows would have to be bought out. So the bill was growing before the bridge was even built.

Even so, the bridge had strong support. The United States Navy, which operated the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard at Bremerton, was a major backer of the plan. The United States Army, which ran McChord Field and Fort Lewis near Tacoma, was behind it as well. So the bridge had the backing of both military branches. Still, the question remained: how would such a large bridge be built, and who would pay for it?

Now a design was needed. Washington State engineer Clark Eldridge prepared a preliminary, tested and conventional suspension bridge design. The Toll Bridge Authority asked the federal Public Works Administration, or PWA, for 11 million dollars, which is equal to about 233 million dollars today. The Washington Department of Highways plans called for trusses 25 feet deep beneath the roadway to stiffen the deck. Keep that in mind. But the story was about to take a turn, as a new approach appeared that could make the bridge both cheaper and more beautiful.

articleEn: Eldridge's design faced a major challenge. Leon Moisseiff, a New York bridge engineer whom Eldridge called one of the "Eastern consulting engineers," went to the PWA and the RFC and asked that the bridge be built at lower cost. Moisseiff was no ordinary name. He had been the designer and a consulting engineer of the Golden Gate Bridge. Born in Riga in 1872, he came to America in 1891 and earned a civil engineering degree from Columbia University in 1895. He made his name in New York, where he was among the designers of the Manhattan Bridge and also helped design the Benjamin Franklin Bridge. In 1933 he received the Franklin Institute's Louis E. Levy Medal. He was famous for deflection theory, the idea that the longer a bridge is, the more flexible it can be. His ideas were carried further by Charles Alton Ellis and used in the design of the Golden Gate Bridge.

Moisseiff was the consulting engineer for this bridge. He and Frederick Lienhard had published a paper that is regarded as perhaps the most important theoretical advance in bridge engineering of the decade. Their theory of elastic distribution extended the deflection theory of the Austrian engineer Josef Melan and carried it to horizontal bending. According to the theory, the stiffness of the main cables could absorb at most half of the static wind pressure, and the force would then pass to the anchorages and towers.

On this basis, Moisseiff proposed plate girders only 8 feet deep instead of the 25-foot trusses. Put simply, an 8-foot deck was more than three times thinner than a 25-foot one. On paper it looked like a clever saving. It would make the bridge slimmer and more elegant, and lower the construction cost. Eldridge's design was judged too expensive, so Moisseiff's won.

On 23 June 1938, the PWA approved about 6 million dollars. Another 1.6 million dollars was to come from tolls, and the estimated total cost was 8 million dollars. Sources differ on when construction began: one gives September 1938, another 23 November 1938. Construction took only 19 months. The cost was 6.4 million dollars, met by the PWA grant and a loan from the Reconstruction Finance Corporation.

Moisseiff, who was the leading engineer on a bridge for the first time, called it the "most beautiful bridge in the world." But not everyone was so confident. In 1938, at a meeting of the American Society of Civil Engineers while the bridge was under construction, David Steinman openly predicted its failure. The bridge's designer was in the audience. Was it only a guess, or a real danger? The bridge itself would give the answer.

articleEn: The bridge was officially named the Tacoma Narrows Bridge, but history remembers it by another name: Galloping Gertie. How did it get that name? First, consider its size. Its main span was 2,800 feet long, about 850 meters. At the time it was the third-longest suspension bridge in the world, behind only the Golden Gate Bridge and the George Washington Bridge.

But for its length, the bridge was very narrow. Because planners expected light traffic, it had only two lanes. It was just 39 feet wide, about 12 meters. Think of that: such a small width for a span of 2,800 feet. The deck was also shallow, supported by plate girders only 8 feet deep. As a result, the deck was not stiff enough, and it began to move easily whenever the wind blew.

And the movement did not start suddenly. While the deck was still being built, it was already moving vertically up and down on windy days. The construction workers noticed the motion and nicknamed the bridge "Galloping Gertie." The name stuck. Construction was completed at the end of June 1940, and on 1 July 1940 the bridge opened to general traffic. The design was Leon Moisseiff's, chosen because the other design was thought too expensive.

On opening day, ordinary people who paid the toll to cross felt the motion as well, and the bridge became famous on its very first day. Even a light to moderate wind was enough. The two halves of the central span could be seen rising and falling by several feet in turn, a cycle repeated every four to five seconds. One half would rise while the other dropped. Drivers watched oncoming cars go up and down as if riding a wave.

Even so, it was believed at the time that the bridge's own weight was enough to keep it safe. That belief later proved costly. An interesting point is that, according to Moisseiff's deflection theory, the longer the bridge, the more flexible it could be. But so far Gertie's motion was up and down. A twisting motion, never seen before, was only four months away. So the question was how to stop the swaying bridge. Engineers tried several methods, which we will look at in the next part.

articleEn: Now the question was how to tame Gertie. While the bridge was still being built, when the deck began moving up and down a great deal, several fixes were tried. The first was tie-down cables, connected to the plate girders and anchored to 50-ton concrete blocks placed on the shore. Their aim was to reduce the deck's motion. But the cables snapped shortly after being installed.

The second fix was a pair of tilted cable stays that joined the main cables to the deck at mid-span. They remained in place until the bridge fell, but they also failed to reduce the oscillations, and the bridge kept moving up and down. The third fix was hydraulic buffers, placed between the towers and the deck's floor system to dampen the longitudinal motion of the main span. But one problem made them useless: when the bridge was sandblasted before painting, the seals of these units were damaged. None of these measures stopped the motion that continued after the bridge opened. The bridge stayed open and traffic kept flowing. Three attempts had been made, and all three had failed.

The Washington State Toll Bridge Authority then called in a professor for help: Frederick Burt Farquharson, a professor of engineering at the University of Washington. He was given the job of running wind tunnel tests and proposing solutions. Farquharson and his students built a 1:200 scale model of the bridge and a 1:20 scale model of a section of the deck. These models were tested in the wind to understand why the bridge moved and how to reduce it.

The first studies were completed on 2 November 1940, just five days before the collapse. The clock was moving fast. Farquharson offered two solutions. The first was to drill holes in the side girders and the deck so that wind could pass through, reducing the lift forces. But this method was irreversible: once done, it could not be undone. The second was to make the deck's shape more aerodynamic by attaching fairings or deflector vanes to the edges of the girders. The first method was rejected for that reason. The second was chosen but never carried out, because the bridge fell five days after the studies ended. The cure had been proposed, but there was no time to apply it.
And then the morning of 7 November arrived. The wind, which had been a nuisance until then, was about to become the bridge's final test.

articleEn: At about 9:45 on the morning of 7 November 1940, especially strong winds began shaking the bridge violently from side to side. Sources differ slightly on the wind speed: one says about 40 miles per hour, another 42. At least two vehicles were on the bridge. One was a delivery truck carrying Ruby Jacox and Arthur Hagen, employees of the Rapid Transfer Company. The other was driven by Leonard Coatsworth, editor of The News Tribune. The shaking overturned the truck, and the car slid uncontrollably from side to side. Jacox, Hagen and Coatsworth all got out of their vehicles and made their way off the bridge on foot.

But Tubby, the dog belonging to Coatsworth's daughter, had been left inside the car. Coatsworth later said he could hear concrete cracking around him. He went back toward the car to get Tubby, but the movement of the bridge would not let him reach it. He realized the bridge was breaking up and that the shore was now the only hope. Mostly on his hands and knees, he covered more than 500 yards, or 460 meters, to the towers. Finally he stood up and even ran a few yards at a time. Then he reached the toll plaza. Traffic was stopped so no more cars would go onto the bridge.

Around then, Howard Clifford, a photographer for the Tacoma News Tribune, walked out onto the bridge to try to rescue Tubby. But when the span began to break in the middle, he had to turn back. The attempt to save Tubby did not succeed.

What was actually happening inside the bridge? For the first time, an entirely new type of motion appeared, called torsional vibration. When the left side of the deck went down, the right side went up, and then the reverse. The two halves twisted in opposite directions. The center line of the road stayed still while the two edges rose and fell in turn. According to Farquharson, this motion was 12 cycles per minute. With every cycle the amplitude grew. Eventually the motion exceeded the strength of the suspender cables. When some cables broke, the deck's weight shifted to the neighboring cables. They too were overloaded and snapped, and the chain reaction continued.

So at about 11 o'clock, almost the entire central deck fell into the waters of Puget Sound. From the toll plaza, Coatsworth watched his car fall too. Tubby did not survive. Later the Washington State Toll Bridge Authority paid Coatsworth 814.40 dollars for the car and its contents.

This raises a big question: how could a new bridge fail like this in only four months? A board of experts met to find the answer. Did they find the truth, or did the matter become more tangled than before?

articleEn: We can see this disaster today only because someone captured it on film. That was done by Barney Elliott and Harbine Monroe, both owners of The Camera Shop in Tacoma. They filmed with two cameras, and the footage included the failed attempt to rescue Tubby. It was shot on 16 mm Kodachrome film, which means the original recording was in color, even though most people today see it in black and white.

The footage was then sold to Paramount Pictures. Paramount made copies and distributed it to cinemas around the world as newsreels. For the newsreels the film was copied onto 35 mm black and white stock, which is why most copies in circulation are not in color.

There is also an interesting technical problem. The two cameras ran at different speeds. Monroe filmed at 24 frames per second, while Elliott filmed at 16. During later conversion it was assumed that the film had been shot at 24 fps, when in fact it was shot at 16. As a result, in most circulating copies the bridge appears to sway about 50 percent faster than it really did. In reality the motion was slower.

In 1998 the Library of Congress selected the film for the National Film Registry because of its cultural and historical importance. In February 2019, another reel came to light. This footage by Arthur Leach is among a few well-known images taken from the Gig Harbor side, the west. Leach was a civil engineer and also a toll collector for the bridge. He is believed to have been the last person to cross the bridge westbound before the collapse. His own commentary can be heard in the footage. It was originally black and white film that was later recorded onto a video cassette.
Today the video is shown to students of engineering, architecture and physics as a cautionary tale. But the question remains: what actually broke the bridge?

articleEn: The Federal Works Agency commission included Othmar Ammann, Theodore von Kármán and Glenn B. Woodruff. Their job was to find the cause of the collapse. But the commission reached no definitive conclusion. It examined three possible causes. The first was aerodynamic instability, meaning self-induced vibrations in the structure. The second was eddy formations, which might be periodic. The third was the random effects of turbulence, meaning irregular ups and downs in wind speed. Today the collapse is generally explained by flutter.

Research also turned up something else. According to Theodore von Kármán, Washington State could not collect on one of the bridge's insurance policies, because the agent, Hallett R. French, had kept the premiums himself. He was tried for grand larceny in connection with the premiums on 800,000 dollars of insurance. The remaining policies covered 80 percent of the bridge's value, and most of that money was collected without trouble.

Now to the science. The bridge failed through aeroelastic flutter. In flutter, several degrees of freedom of the structure couple together with the force of the wind to produce unstable oscillation. Aeroelasticity is the field that studies the relationship among inertial, elastic and aerodynamic forces when a flexible body is in a fluid flow. The trouble with flutter is that the forces do not restrain themselves, and the motion keeps growing. Eventually the amplitude became too great for the suspender cables to bear.

One key point is negative damping. In any steady wind above about 35 miles per hour, the amplitude of torsional flutter would keep growing. Normally damping reduces motion. Here the damping factor was negative, meaning the effect was reversed and was increasing the motion.

Now for the famous misconception. Many physics textbooks say the bridge failed because of resonance. Billah and Scanlan showed in 1991 that this explanation is wrong. It was said that the frequency of the wind's vortices, the Kármán vortex street, matched the bridge's natural frequency. That was a theory, not fact. According to Farquharson, the wind was steady at 42 miles per hour, and the frequency of the destructive motion was 12 cycles per minute, or 0.2 Hz. At that speed the vortex shedding frequency of a bluff body would be about 1 Hz. So the two frequencies did not match, and vortex shedding was not the cause. The Federal Works Administration report found no sharp correlation between wind velocity and oscillation frequency, which would be necessary for resonance with vortices. According to Billah and Scanlan, this was wind-driven amplification, which keeps growing as wind speed increases, unlike resonance.

So is the debate over? Not entirely, because there is no single agreed definition of resonance, so the debate remains to some extent. Billah and Scanlan wrote that if periodic impulses are taken to be self-induced, it may be possible to call it resonance. But that is quite different from externally forced linear resonance. In other words, the wind supplied the power, and the bridge's own motion created a way to draw that power in. The question is what this lesson changed afterward.

Clark Eldridge: 1930s Washington state engineer, serious man in a dark suit with blueprints. Leon Moisseiff: late 1930s, elderly bridge engineer in a dark suit with round glasses, grey hair. Frederick Burt Farquharson: 1940, university professor in a tweed jacket beside a small wind tunnel bridge model. Theodore von Karman: 1940s, aerodynamicist in a suit at a chalkboard. Tubby: small black Cocker Spaniel (shown only in a calm, safe way). Barney Elliott and Harbine Monroe: 1940, camera shop owners with a 16 mm film camera on a tripod, in coats and hats. Replacement 1950 bridge: wide deck with deep open steel truss.

articleEn: Gertie's fallen deck still serves as an artificial reef beneath Puget Sound and is listed on the National Register of Historic Places. Efforts to clear and salvage the wreckage continued until May 1943. Two review boards said the bridge could not be repaired, so the whole superstructure would have to be rebuilt. Steel was precious in wartime, so the cables and span steel were sold as scrap. But the salvage left the state with a net loss of more than 350,000 dollars.

Moisseiff's reputation was badly damaged by the disaster. He died of a heart attack in 1943. His son believed the bridge's failure contributed to his death. Yet the failure spurred a movement to improve suspension bridge design. Othmar Ammann wrote that bridge engineering is not an exact science, and that when engineers venture into new territory, neither theory nor experience can give complete guidance. After this, engineers made aerodynamics part of design, and wind tunnel testing eventually became mandatory.
The Bronx–Whitestone Bridge was also reinforced soon after. In 1943, steel trusses 14 feet high were added to it, and in 2003 they were removed and replaced with aerodynamic fiberglass fairings.

The new Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened on 14 October 1950. It reused Gertie's tower pedestals and cable anchorages, but the deck was completely different. Instead of a thin plate girder, it now had an open stiffening truss 33 feet deep. Open wind grates 3 inches deep were also placed between the lanes. In the 1960s came box girder bridges, shaped like airfoils, such as the Severn Bridge. They provided the necessary stiffness and also reduced torsional forces. In July 2007 a second, parallel bridge opened, carrying eastbound traffic, while the 1950 bridge now carries westbound traffic.

Finally, an open question. The aeroelastic forces among wind, bridge and fluid flow are very complicated. Do we still fully understand them in every design today? If you enjoyed this story, like the video, subscribe to the channel, and tell us which story should come next.

shorts.titleEn: The Morning a Bridge Threw Cars Off Balance
shorts.text: 7 نومبر 1940 کی صبح ایک پل نے سڑک پر چلتی گاڑی کو بے قابو کر دیا۔ جگہ تھی Washington State کا Tacoma Narrows۔ وقت تھا تقریباً 9:45 بجے۔ تیز ہوا چل رہی تھی، اور نیا suspension bridge دائیں بائیں جھول رہا تھا۔ پل پر کم از کم دو گاڑیاں تھیں۔ ایک delivery truck الٹ گیا۔ دوسری گاڑی The News Tribune کے editor Leonard Coatsworth چلا رہے تھے، اور وہ سڑک پر پھسلنے لگی۔ Coatsworth گاڑی چھوڑ کر پیدل نکلے۔ وہ ہاتھوں اور گھٹنوں کے بل 500 yards سے زیادہ فاصلہ طے کر کے towers تک پہنچے۔ Ruby Jacox اور Arthur Hagen بھی پیدل پل سے اتر گئے۔ مگر گاڑی میں ایک چھوٹا سا مسافر رہ گیا تھا۔ وہ کون تھا؟ اور پل کا آخر کیا بنا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: 7 November 1940 ki subah ek pul ne sadak par chalti gaadi ko be qaabu kar diya. Jagah thi Washington State ka Tacoma Narrows. Waqt tha taqriban 9:45 baje. Tez hawa chal rahi thi, aur naya suspension bridge daayen baayen jhool raha tha. Pul par kam az kam do gaariyan thin. Ek delivery truck ulat gaya. Doosri gaari The News Tribune ke editor Leonard Coatsworth chala rahe thay, aur woh sadak par phisalne lagi. Coatsworth gaadi chhor kar paidal nikle. Woh haathon aur ghutnon ke bal 500 yards se zyada faasla tay kar ke towers tak pohanche. Ruby Jacox aur Arthur Hagen bhi paidal pul se utar gaye. Magar gaadi mein ek chhota sa musafir reh gaya tha. Woh kaun tha? Aur pul ka aakhir kya bana? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: On 7 November 1940 the Tacoma Narrows Bridge swayed wildly in the wind. Leonard Coatsworth and two truck workers had to leave their vehicles and walk off the bridge.

shorts.titleEn: 3 Fixes That All Failed on Galloping Gertie
shorts.text: پل کو بچانے کے لیے تین حل آزمائے گئے، اور تینوں ناکام رہے۔ کیسے؟ تعمیر کے دوران ہی deck بہت اوپر نیچے ہو رہا تھا۔ پہلا حل تھا tie-down cables۔ انہیں 50 ton کے concrete blocks سے باندھا گیا۔ مگر cables لگنے کے تھوڑی دیر بعد ٹوٹ گئیں۔ دوسرا حل تھا دو tilted cable stays۔ یہ پل گرنے تک لگی رہیں، لیکن oscillations کم نہ کر سکیں۔ تیسرا حل تھا hydraulic buffers۔ ان کی seals sand-blasting کے دوران خراب ہو گئیں، اور ان کا اثر ختم ہو گیا۔ پھر University of Washington کے Professor Farquharson نے wind tunnel tests کیے۔ ان کی پہلی studies 2 نومبر 1940 کو مکمل ہوئیں۔ پل گرنے میں کتنے دن باقی تھے؟ صرف 5۔ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Pul ko bachane ke liye teen hal azmaye gaye, aur teeno nakaam rahe. Kaise? Tameer ke dauran hi deck bohat upar neeche ho raha tha. Pehla hal tha tie-down cables. Unhein 50 ton ke concrete blocks se bandha gaya. Magar cables lagne ke thori der baad toot gayin. Doosra hal tha do tilted cable stays. Yeh pul girne tak lagi rahin, lekin oscillations kam na kar saki. Teesra hal tha hydraulic buffers. Un ki seals sand-blasting ke dauran kharab ho gayin, aur un ka asar khatam ho gaya. Phir University of Washington ke Professor Farquharson ne wind tunnel tests kiye. Un ki pehli studies 2 November 1940 ko mukammal huin. Pul girne mein kitne din baqi thay? Sirf 5. Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: Engineers tried tie-down cables, cable stays and hydraulic buffers to calm Galloping Gertie. None worked, and the wind tunnel study finished just five days before the collapse.

shorts.titleEn: The Famous Collapse Film Has a Hidden Speed Error
shorts.text: اس تباہی کی فلم آج بھی دنیا بھر میں دکھائی جاتی ہے، مگر اس میں ایک چھپی ہوئی گڑبڑ ہے۔ دوستو، یہ footage Barney Elliott اور Harbine Monroe نے بنائی تھی۔ دونوں Tacoma میں The Camera Shop کے مالک تھے۔ انہوں نے دو cameras استعمال کیے۔ فلم 16 mm Kodachrome پر بنی تھی، یعنی اصل recording colour میں تھی۔ پھر یہ footage Paramount Pictures کو بیچی گئی۔ newsreels کے لیے اسے 35 mm black and white stock پر copy کیا گیا۔ اسی لیے آج زیادہ تر لوگ اسے black and white میں دیکھتے ہیں۔ 1998 میں اسے National Film Registry میں محفوظ کیا گیا۔ Monroe 24 frames per second پر film کر رہے تھے، اور Elliott 16 پر۔ conversion میں سب کو 24 مان لیا گیا۔ تو پل اصل سے کتنا تیز ہلتا دکھتا ہے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Is tabahi ki film aaj bhi duniya bhar mein dikhai jati hai, magar is mein ek chhupi hui gadbad hai. Dosto, yeh footage Barney Elliott aur Harbine Monroe ne banayi thi. Dono Tacoma mein The Camera Shop ke malik thay. Unhon ne do cameras istemal kiye. Film 16 mm Kodachrome par bani thi, yani asal recording colour mein thi. Phir yeh footage Paramount Pictures ko bechi gayi. newsreels ke liye ise 35 mm black and white stock par copy kiya gaya. Isi liye aaj zyada tar log ise black and white mein dekhte hain. 1998 mein ise National Film Registry mein mehfooz kiya gaya. Monroe 24 frames per second par film kar rahe thay, aur Elliott 16 par. conversion mein sab ko 24 maan liya gaya. To pul asal se kitna tez hilta dikhta hai? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn: The famous footage of the Tacoma Narrows collapse was shot on colour film by two Tacoma shop owners. Because of a frame-rate assumption, most copies show the bridge moving faster than it really did.
